newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks edge ahead to new record close.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks edge ahead to new record close.

text.p: Mexican stocks overcame late profit-taking and edged higher to their third straight record Friday.
The IPC share index rose 4.61 points to 4,244.63. Volume was heavy at 165.7 million shares and pointed to strong demand from foreign investors, analysts said.
"My read is there's lots of equity money flowing in from the States, as fears of a rates hike in the U.S. diminish," said Felix Boni, head of research at ING-Barings in Mexico.
Boni said a drop in U.S. producer prices in May reported Friday encouraged the view increases in U.S. interest rates for the second half of 1997 would be restrained.
"If you want to know what the market is thinking on interest rates, just look at the Dow Jones," said Ramon Ruiz, a sales trader at Latinvest in New York.

The Dow Jones industrial average rose 70.57 points to 7,782.04, its sixth straight record. The 30-year U.S. Treasury rose 20/32, or $6.25 on a $1,000 bond, sending its yield down to 6.73 percent from 6.78 percent Thursday. The price and the yield move in opposite directions.
Mexico's blue-chip IPC had risen as high as 4,291.11 points in early trade, before profit-takers stepped in, dealers said.
"They were taking profits, I mean we've had a streak of record closes, so it was a good time to do so. The market still feels firm, though," a floor trader said.
The trader said profit-taking was most evident in Telmex and glassmaker Vitro.
Telmex ended down 10 centavos (1 cent) at 18.90 pesos ($2.37), but had earlier risen to a peso record of 19.24 pesos.

The telecomms stock's ADRs ended down 1/4 at 47-3/8, having declined from a year high of 48-3/8, a level not seen since the December 1994 devaluation crisis. Telmex ADRs reached a peak of more than 70 in February 1994.
Vitro ended the day up 1.40 pesos (18 cents) at 26.60 pesos ($3.34), but down from a year high of 27.50 pesos ($3.46) reached earlier in the day.
Bank stocks gained on speculation about a possible government plan to restructure banks' past-due loans.
Bancomer, one of Mexico's biggest banks, unseated Telmex from its customary first place on the most-traded stocks list.
Bancomer common shares rose 30 centavos to 3.70 pesos, while the preferred "A" shares ended up 9 centavos (1 cent) to 1.97 pesos (25 cents).
On the broad market, of 122 stocks traded, gainers outnumbered decliners by 59 to 37.
